paras: The attempted lynchings of Tom Hayes were two efforts by crowds in Covington County, Alabama, in the summer of 1910 to seize and kill Hayes, a Black man accused of murdering R. D. Sowell, a white night watchman at a lumber yard near Andalusia. On July 31 a crowd of mill workers pursued the officers' automobile carrying Hayes to the railroad station at Gantt, and on the night of August 24 a mob reported at 250 men planned to storm the Andalusia jail. Hayes escaped both times, by automobile and train on the first occasion and under a militia guard on the second, and was held in the Montgomery County jail.

Sowell, a watchman of about thirty-five, was found dead on Sunday, July 31, with a knife in his throat, at the lumber yard where he worked. The Montgomery Advertiser placed the killing early Sunday morning and named his employer as the Empire Lumber Company, while a Pensacola Journal correspondent said it happened Saturday night at the Foshee & McGowan mill. Suspicion fell on Hayes because the knife was thought to be his; he had twice been charged under the liquor laws and had been discharged by the company. Other reports said Sowell had been a witness against Hayes for selling whiskey, and the Pensacola paper called Hayes a "blind tiger" negro.

When the body was found, the "mill operatives became enraged" and started after Hayes, whom Sheriff Prestwood had arrested at his home without resistance. Followed by what the Advertiser called "an ever increasing crowd of anygry men," Deputy Sheriff J. M. Johnson raced Hayes by automobile to Gantt, nine miles away, and took him by train to Montgomery, arriving that evening. At the Montgomery jail Hayes said he had not killed Sowell.

After ten days in Montgomery, Hayes was taken back to Andalusia on Monday, August 22, for trial, in the custody of Sheriff Prestwood. Sheriff Horace Hood of Montgomery reported that prisoners had seen Hayes washing a bloody undershirt and that Hayes had confessed, an account that came from the officers. According to Sheriff Prestwood, he heard on Tuesday night that a mob would storm the jail, and on Wednesday night, August 24, he learned that 250 men had organized several miles from town. He called out the local militia company to surround the jail, and an advance party of about twenty-five or thirty men rode up, saw the guard and left. On the morning of August 25 Hayes was sent back to the Montgomery jail on the first train.

The Advertiser said Hayes would probably stay in Montgomery until his trial, and the Age-Herald warned that if he were taken back he would "likely be killed." No arrest of anyone in either crowd is reported, and no report of Hayes's trial was found in the coverage through September.

Only white newspapers carried the episode, chiefly the Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Pensacola Journal, with a short wire item in the Bamberg Herald of South Carolina. The Advertiser's first report described the crowd as enraged mill workers and credited only the automobile with keeping Hayes from a crowd "bent upon lynching," and the Pensacola correspondent likewise wrote that "only the precaution of the sheriff" saved him. When Hayes was returned to Andalusia, the papers treated a lynching as likely: the Associated Press headline read "Take Negro to Danger Zone," and the Age-Herald wrote that "the belief was general" he would be lynched.

Several items stated Hayes's guilt as fact, the Age-Herald writing that he "killed" Sowell, and repeated the jail confession and bloody undershirt from Sheriff Hood. The second attempt was framed as a sheriff's success, under the Advertiser headline "Sheriff Foils Plans of Mob" and the Pensacola headline "Narrow Escape From Lynching." No Black-press report of the episode was found.

Accounts differ on the hour of the killing, Sowell's employer, the motive (a whiskey case or a pawned pistol) and the train's destination, which one wire brief gave as Troy rather than Montgomery. Versions of the August mob's timing, all from Sheriff Prestwood, differ: the Advertiser said it planned to strike at 2 a.m., the Age-Herald that he was warned about 2 p.m.

reader.title: Attempted lynchings of Tom Hayes
bases: A crowd of mill operatives pursued the sheriff's automobile carrying Hayes on July 31 (A1, A3), and a mob reported at 250 men planned to storm the Andalusia jail on August 24-25 (A9, A10, A11); neither reached him.

Hayes was not killed: officers outran the July 31 crowd (A1, A3) and militia guarding the jail turned back the August 24-25 mob (A9, A11); both were groups acting on the accusation that he had murdered Sowell, so the episode is an attempted lynching.

The July 31 pursuit is reported independently by the Montgomery Advertiser and a Pensacola Journal special (A1, A3) and the August 24-25 jail threat by the Advertiser, the Age-Herald and the Associated Press (A9, A10, A11).

accounts.label: Andalusia correspondents
accounts.gist: Angry mill operatives chased the sheriff's automobile to Gantt station, and only the car and the sheriff's precaution kept Hayes from a crowd 'bent upon lynching'.

accounts.label: Sheriff Hood (Montgomery)
accounts.gist: Fellow prisoners saw Hayes washing a bloody undershirt and Hayes later confessed to the sheriff; this is the officers' account.

accounts.label: Sheriff Prestwood
accounts.gist: He learned that a mob had formed outside Andalusia, called out the militia, and an advance party of about 25 rode up, saw the guard and left.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser headlined 'Negro Rushed to County Jail' and 'Sheriff Foils Plans of Mob', describing the crowd as enraged mill operatives without endorsing it.
The Birmingham Age-Herald stated that Hayes 'killed' Sowell as fact and called the jail inmates 'bad boarders', while reporting his escape from the mob as owed to the sheriff.
The Pensacola Journal ran AP items headed 'Take Negro to Danger Zone' and 'Narrow Escape From Lynching', and the Bamberg Herald a short wire brief.

conflicts.note: All agree the body was found on Sunday, July 31.
Most reports, including both Montgomery papers, name the Empire Lumber Company.
The Advertiser reports the deputy's arrival at the Montgomery jail that evening, and later items say Hayes spent ten days there, so Montgomery is better supported.
